medical.title: Breathing without brakes: An unexpected cause of Rett syndrome symptoms
medical.summary: Hyperventilating. Breath-holding until they turn blue. This abnormal breathing is frequent and disturbing in people with Rett syndrome, a rare genetic disease. Now University of Connecticut researchers report in Current Biology why those episodes happen and show how medications for an entirely different disease might help.

medical.title: Berry compound reduces fat buildup in muscle cells, study finds
medical.summary: Ectopic lipid accumulation in skeletal muscle is a major health concern driven by factors like high-fat diets, lack of exercise and aging. Unlike subcutaneous fat, these intracellular lipid droplets interfere with normal muscle function and reduce the body's ability to efficiently use glucose and fatty acids. This condition impairs metabolic flexibility and leads to insulin resistance. Therefore, finding ways to control excessive lipid buildup in skeletal muscle is crucial for extending a healthy lifespan and preventing lifestyle-related disorders.

medical.title: GLP-1 treatment late in life extends lifespan in animal model
medical.summary: A study published in Nature has shown that the GLP-1 drug semaglutide extended the lifespan of older, healthy mice by tempering the detrimental effects of aging. Researchers at the University of California, Berkeley, directly compared the effects of the treatment with those of reduced food intake. They found that the drug mimicked the anti-aging benefits of calorie restriction, conferring even greater benefits in some areas.

medical.title: Level of education most strongly linked to survival after hip fracture
medical.summary: Level of education is the socioeconomic factor most strongly associated with survival rates after acute hip surgery. This is shown in a Linköping University study of 58,000 people. The results can be used to better identify patients who may need more support after surgery.

medical.title: Genetics of personality may shape more life outcomes than previously thought
medical.summary: An international consortium of researchers found that more than 1,200 different genetic variants are associated with the Big Five personality traits—and, surprisingly, these personality genetics are linked to dozens of life outcomes.

medical.title: Musicians' brains stay one step ahead, study finds
medical.summary: Musicians don't just learn movement sequences faster; they predict what's coming next sooner, according to new research that also found newly formed motor memories can be disrupted by seeing different visual sequences shortly after learning. The work is published in the journal Psychological Research.

medical.title: Money problems may age your brain faster
medical.summary: Persistent financial hardship in early and middle adulthood was linked to poorer thinking skills by the 50s and more signs of brain aging later in life. Researchers say years of chronic stress and financial worry may gradually take a toll on the brain.

medical.title: Expanding telehealth access calls for stronger physician support
medical.summary: Telehealth has transformed health care access, making it easier for millions of patients to connect with physicians without leaving home. New research from the University of Miami Business School finds that sustaining those gains will require health systems to address the operational demands virtual care can place on physicians.

medical.title: Urine test identifies more than nine in ten bladder cancers, clinical study finds
medical.summary: New research has found that more than 9 in 10 patients with bladder cancer were identified through a noninvasive urine test after urgent referral. The study, led by the University of Birmingham and Nonacus Ltd., involved 964 patients across seven NHS urology departments to examine the real-world significance of testing for bladder cancer using a commercially available urine test. GALEAS™ Bladder, which tests genomic information from a patient's urine for traces of bladder cancer, detected 71 of 77 cancers (92.2%) among the nearly 1,000 patients.

medical.title: Could skin reveal new clues about aging and frailty?
medical.summary: When it comes to aging skin, scientists think of much more than wrinkles. They think of an organ with multitudes of microbes, immune cells, structural proteins and chemical signals that constantly interact with one another.

medical.title: Painful periods during adolescence linked to symptoms years earlier
medical.summary: More than half of girls participating in the long-term U.S. Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) study developed painful periods (dysmenorrhea) by age 12 or 13, according to new research published in The Lancet Child & Adolescent Health. Black and Hispanic girls were most likely to be affected.

medical.title: Alzheimer’s may leave a mark on the brain long before plaques appear
medical.summary: Brain changes associated with Alzheimer’s may begin at least seven years before amyloid plaques become detectable with current PET scans. Researchers uncovered the signal by tracking healthy older adults with repeated brain imaging over nearly 20 years. The discovery could help scientists identify Alzheimer’s earlier and suggests that important disease processes may start before visible plaque buildup.

medical.title: Psychologists investigate how first impressions influence impressions of trustworthiness
medical.summary: First impressions of whether someone appears trustworthy are influenced by the faces we have just seen, according to new research from psychologists at the University of Aberdeen. The study is the first to show that our snap judgments of trustworthiness are not based solely on the face in front of us. Instead, they are subtly shaped by the faces we have encountered only moments earlier.

medical.title: Understanding the link between hepatitis C and HIV persistence
medical.summary: Naglaa Shoukry and Petronela Ancuta, researchers in the Immunopathology Research Theme at the Centre de recherche du CHUM (CRCHUM), are shedding new light on one of the greatest challenges in HIV research: understanding why the virus remains in the body despite treatment.

medical.title: First human clinical trial to test precision form of FLASH proton therapy
medical.summary: A new form of proton therapy—designed to deliver cancer-killing radiation therapy in less than a second, through fewer sessions, with potentially less risk of damaging side effects—is now being tested in a phase 1 clinical trial at the Abramson Cancer Center of the University of Pennsylvania. Known as FLASH proton therapy, the feasibility study represents the first time that the "conformal," or precise 3D targeting, version of the technique has been tested in human patients in the United States.

medical.title: Is sleep training likely to help or harm your baby?
medical.summary: Welcoming a baby is a time of great joy for parents. It can also be one of the most challenging. One of the greatest difficulties many parents face is getting their baby to sleep and resettling them following nighttime awakenings.

medical.title: Irritability, anxiety and negative thought patterns in ADHD associated with increased depression risk
medical.summary: A new study by the Wolfson Center at Cardiff University investigating links between ADHD and depression has shown that underlying factors such as anxiety and negative thought patterns in childhood, adolescence and young adulthood indicate depression risk. The research team suggests that identifying these emotions, behaviors and beliefs in children and young people with ADHD could be a promising intervention for preventing future depression in these individuals.

science.title: Exotic pines in the Southern Hemisphere grow faster and are more drought-resistant, study reveals
science.summary: A new study published in the journal Nature reveals that conifers planted outside their native range in the Southern Hemisphere not only grow up to four times faster than those in the Northern Hemisphere but also show greater resistance and resilience to drought. The finding challenges one of the most deeply rooted ideas in plant ecology: that plants that grow rapidly generally have a lower capacity to tolerate water stress.

science.title: Electric fish keep from blinding themselves with these brain cells
science.summary: The brain cells you see in the above image help an African fish decode electric signals to spot prey, scan its murky surroundings and communicate with its fellows. By rigorously mapping how these cells in the electrosensory lobe are wired together, scientists at Columbia's Zuckerman Institute and their colleagues reveal how this brain area continually learns to filter out interference that would otherwise blind the fish's electric sense. They report their findings in Nature.

science.title: New clustering method uncovers hidden regularities in data
science.summary: One dataset, one model? This approach does not always produce the most useful insights, as a dataset often contains many different relationships. To better understand them, researchers at the Paluno Research Institute in the Faculty of Computer Science at the University of Duisburg-Essen have developed a method that clusters data according to mathematical functions. The key feature is that neither the number and structure of the functions nor the assignment of data points to them needs to be known in advance.

science.title: Mammalian genes can combine to make previously unknown mRNAs and proteins
science.summary: For decades, scientists have understood that each of the roughly 20,000 genes in the human body carries instructions for a single kind of protein. Now, researchers at Harvard Medical School have discovered that instructions from different genes—even those on different chromosomes—can combine to create chimeric mRNAs that produce previously unknown, functional proteins.

science.title: Interstellar solar sails hit a strange problem at 75% of light speed
science.summary: Solar sails pushed by powerful lasers could reach incredible speeds, but relativity may eventually make the light itself work against them. At around 75% of the speed of light, scattered photons can begin creating drag, adding a surprising obstacle to interstellar travel.

science.title: Why lower-class workers are less likely to negotiate for higher pay—and how it could cost some nearly $800,000
science.summary: Michele Gelfand has studied and taught negotiation for years. A professor of organizational behavior at Stanford Graduate School of Business, she sees negotiation as a skill that is imperative for everyone to learn. "It's not something we're born with," she says. "It's something we learn over time."

science.title: Hawai'i high school students name image of glittering galaxy pair
science.summary: Nā ʻUhane Māhoe Huki Pū i ke Ola is the Hawaiian name given to NGC 7253—a pair of spiral galaxies caught in each other's gravity. Captured by the Gemini North telescope on Maunakea in Hawai'i, the image created a spectacular symbolic display for this year's interns participating in Project Hōkūlani.

science.title: Bio-based plastic turns into fertilizer after use
science.summary: Plastic waste is one of the world's fastest-growing environmental problems. According to the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development's Global Plastics Outlook: Policy Scenarios to 2060 report, global plastic use is projected to nearly triple from 460 million metric tons in 2019 to 1.2 billion metric tons by 2060 if current trends continue.

science.title: DNA testing shows what's really in Western Australian fish and chip shop 'shark' filets
science.summary: Shark products sold at Western Australian fish-and-chips shops are often labeled too ambiguously or, in some cases, mislabeled, leaving consumers unsure which species they are buying, new Murdoch University research shows.

science.title: A 13-meter rocket hit the Moon: Tasmanian researchers helped track it there
science.summary: A 13-meter (43-foot) Falcon 9 rocket stage struck the moon last month, leaving a crater about 20 meters (66 feet) wide. In the days before impact, University of Tasmania researchers from the School of Natural Sciences were the first in the world to detect the object by radar, helping refine predictions of where it would land.

science.title: Physicists test the weak equivalence principle in an orbiting space station
science.summary: The weak equivalence principle (WEP) is central to Einstein's general relativity. It posits that gravity must accelerate everything equally, regardless of what it is made from. For the first time, a team led by Ming-Sheng Zhan at the Wuhan Institute of Physics and Mathematics has tested the principle using clouds of continuously free-falling atoms aboard an orbiting space station.

science.title: A coffee-table-size scorpion roamed Earth before forests existed
science.summary: A meter-long scorpion with massive pincers stalked ancient Britain 415 million years ago, long before forests and the better-known age of giant insects. Its surprising size and possible semi-aquatic lifestyle could reshape ideas about how early arthropods became giants.

science.title: A summer odyssey: Female dotterels seek multiple mates across Northern Europe
science.summary: On a high Norwegian plateau in late May, patches of bare ground begin to appear through the snow, and with them arrive some of Europe's most approachable birds. Eurasian dotterels breed on exposed mountain ridges and Arctic tundra from Scotland, through Scandinavia, to Siberia, and are famously tolerant of people—a trait that has long made them easy prey for hunters. They are unusual in another sense, too.

science.title: Despite years of rain, Blue Mountains forests still haven't recovered from the Black Summer megafires
science.summary: For three years before the Black Summer megafires of 2019–20, cool-season rainfall in southeastern Australia was only half the normal amount. When fires broke out, intensely dry conditions helped them spread through areas typically resistant to burning, such as wetlands and rainforests.

science.title: Seven new species show 250-million-year-old marine group is still evolving
science.summary: Scientists believed there were only two species of hornerid bryozoans in Aotearoa New Zealand, but new research shows several more have been secretly evolving and thriving in the nation's southern waters.

science.title: New research: Google's AI Overviews reinforce some conspiracy theories
science.summary: Imagine overhearing on a bus that the city council plans to implement new restrictions under an urban planning program called "15-minute cities." Curious, you search the term on Google.

science.title: More than 120 molecular species found in giant cloud near Milky Way's center
science.summary: Astronomers have discovered a second interstellar cloud near the center of the Milky Way that is extraordinarily rich in complex molecules, including several molecules associated with prebiotic chemistry. The newly studied cloud, G+0.633-0.0604, or G+0.633, contains more than 120 identified molecular species and is the first confirmed chemical twin of another famous molecule-rich cloud. Their paper, posted to the arXiv preprint server on Aug. 14, outlines the chemistry of the newfound cloud.

science.title: Human-like AI not always the answer in customer service
science.summary: The next time something goes wrong with your bank account, package delivery or a bill, there's a good chance you'll be directed to AI for customer service.

environment.title: 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck reveals ancient waterproofing secrets
environment.summary: Scientists analyzing a 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck found that its hull was coated with pine tar and, in one area, a mixture of tar and beeswax. Pollen trapped in those ancient coatings acted like a geographic fingerprint, revealing the landscapes surrounding the ship when repairs were made.

environment.title: A lost mega-cliff may explain the Grand Canyon’s missing billion years
environment.summary: A colossal cliff system created as the supercontinent Rodinia broke apart may have exposed the heart of the Grand Canyon nearly a billion years before the Colorado River carved it. The ancient landscape could also help explain why enormous sections of North America’s geological record appear to be missing.

environment.title: “One-in-a-million” sea creature fossil preserves soft tissue for 450 million years
environment.summary: Scientists have identified exceptionally rare soft tissue preserved in a 450-million-year-old crinoid fossil, more than 200 million years older than the first dinosaurs. Its delicate tube feet offer a remarkable new window into how some of Earth’s earliest reef animals lived, fed, and evolved.

environment.title: A new Ice Age species was hiding in la brea tar pits fossils for decades
environment.summary: Scientists have discovered a new extinct amphibian species hiding in the fossil collections of Los Angeles’ La Brea Tar Pits. Named Spea labreae, the Ice Age spadefoot toad is an exceptionally rare find—only one other extinct Pleistocene amphibian has ever been identified in North America. Its bones had been sitting in collections since the 1950s before a researcher noticed features that set it apart from known species.

mix_items.title: Breathing without brakes: An unexpected cause of Rett syndrome symptoms
mix_items.summary: Hyperventilating. Breath-holding until they turn blue. This abnormal breathing is frequent and disturbing in people with Rett syndrome, a rare genetic disease. Now University of Connecticut researchers report in Current Biology why those episodes happen and show how medications for an entirely different disease might help.

mix_items.title: Berry compound reduces fat buildup in muscle cells, study finds
mix_items.summary: Ectopic lipid accumulation in skeletal muscle is a major health concern driven by factors like high-fat diets, lack of exercise and aging. Unlike subcutaneous fat, these intracellular lipid droplets interfere with normal muscle function and reduce the body's ability to efficiently use glucose and fatty acids. This condition impairs metabolic flexibility and leads to insulin resistance. Therefore, finding ways to control excessive lipid buildup in skeletal muscle is crucial for extending a healthy lifespan and preventing lifestyle-related disorders.

mix_items.title: GLP-1 treatment late in life extends lifespan in animal model
mix_items.summary: A study published in Nature has shown that the GLP-1 drug semaglutide extended the lifespan of older, healthy mice by tempering the detrimental effects of aging. Researchers at the University of California, Berkeley, directly compared the effects of the treatment with those of reduced food intake. They found that the drug mimicked the anti-aging benefits of calorie restriction, conferring even greater benefits in some areas.

mix_items.title: Exotic pines in the Southern Hemisphere grow faster and are more drought-resistant, study reveals
mix_items.summary: A new study published in the journal Nature reveals that conifers planted outside their native range in the Southern Hemisphere not only grow up to four times faster than those in the Northern Hemisphere but also show greater resistance and resilience to drought. The finding challenges one of the most deeply rooted ideas in plant ecology: that plants that grow rapidly generally have a lower capacity to tolerate water stress.

mix_items.title: Electric fish keep from blinding themselves with these brain cells
mix_items.summary: The brain cells you see in the above image help an African fish decode electric signals to spot prey, scan its murky surroundings and communicate with its fellows. By rigorously mapping how these cells in the electrosensory lobe are wired together, scientists at Columbia's Zuckerman Institute and their colleagues reveal how this brain area continually learns to filter out interference that would otherwise blind the fish's electric sense. They report their findings in Nature.

mix_items.title: Level of education most strongly linked to survival after hip fracture
mix_items.summary: Level of education is the socioeconomic factor most strongly associated with survival rates after acute hip surgery. This is shown in a Linköping University study of 58,000 people. The results can be used to better identify patients who may need more support after surgery.

mix_items.title: New clustering method uncovers hidden regularities in data
mix_items.summary: One dataset, one model? This approach does not always produce the most useful insights, as a dataset often contains many different relationships. To better understand them, researchers at the Paluno Research Institute in the Faculty of Computer Science at the University of Duisburg-Essen have developed a method that clusters data according to mathematical functions. The key feature is that neither the number and structure of the functions nor the assignment of data points to them needs to be known in advance.

mix_items.title: Mammalian genes can combine to make previously unknown mRNAs and proteins
mix_items.summary: For decades, scientists have understood that each of the roughly 20,000 genes in the human body carries instructions for a single kind of protein. Now, researchers at Harvard Medical School have discovered that instructions from different genes—even those on different chromosomes—can combine to create chimeric mRNAs that produce previously unknown, functional proteins.

mix_items.title: Genetics of personality may shape more life outcomes than previously thought
mix_items.summary: An international consortium of researchers found that more than 1,200 different genetic variants are associated with the Big Five personality traits—and, surprisingly, these personality genetics are linked to dozens of life outcomes.

mix_items.title: Interstellar solar sails hit a strange problem at 75% of light speed
mix_items.summary: Solar sails pushed by powerful lasers could reach incredible speeds, but relativity may eventually make the light itself work against them. At around 75% of the speed of light, scattered photons can begin creating drag, adding a surprising obstacle to interstellar travel.

mix_items.title: Why lower-class workers are less likely to negotiate for higher pay—and how it could cost some nearly $800,000
mix_items.summary: Michele Gelfand has studied and taught negotiation for years. A professor of organizational behavior at Stanford Graduate School of Business, she sees negotiation as a skill that is imperative for everyone to learn. "It's not something we're born with," she says. "It's something we learn over time."

mix_items.title: Musicians' brains stay one step ahead, study finds
mix_items.summary: Musicians don't just learn movement sequences faster; they predict what's coming next sooner, according to new research that also found newly formed motor memories can be disrupted by seeing different visual sequences shortly after learning. The work is published in the journal Psychological Research.

mix_items.title: Money problems may age your brain faster
mix_items.summary: Persistent financial hardship in early and middle adulthood was linked to poorer thinking skills by the 50s and more signs of brain aging later in life. Researchers say years of chronic stress and financial worry may gradually take a toll on the brain.

mix_items.title: Expanding telehealth access calls for stronger physician support
mix_items.summary: Telehealth has transformed health care access, making it easier for millions of patients to connect with physicians without leaving home. New research from the University of Miami Business School finds that sustaining those gains will require health systems to address the operational demands virtual care can place on physicians.

mix_items.title: Hawai'i high school students name image of glittering galaxy pair
mix_items.summary: Nā ʻUhane Māhoe Huki Pū i ke Ola is the Hawaiian name given to NGC 7253—a pair of spiral galaxies caught in each other's gravity. Captured by the Gemini North telescope on Maunakea in Hawai'i, the image created a spectacular symbolic display for this year's interns participating in Project Hōkūlani.

mix_items.title: Urine test identifies more than nine in ten bladder cancers, clinical study finds
mix_items.summary: New research has found that more than 9 in 10 patients with bladder cancer were identified through a noninvasive urine test after urgent referral. The study, led by the University of Birmingham and Nonacus Ltd., involved 964 patients across seven NHS urology departments to examine the real-world significance of testing for bladder cancer using a commercially available urine test. GALEAS™ Bladder, which tests genomic information from a patient's urine for traces of bladder cancer, detected 71 of 77 cancers (92.2%) among the nearly 1,000 patients.

mix_items.title: Bio-based plastic turns into fertilizer after use
mix_items.summary: Plastic waste is one of the world's fastest-growing environmental problems. According to the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development's Global Plastics Outlook: Policy Scenarios to 2060 report, global plastic use is projected to nearly triple from 460 million metric tons in 2019 to 1.2 billion metric tons by 2060 if current trends continue.

mix_items.title: Could skin reveal new clues about aging and frailty?
mix_items.summary: When it comes to aging skin, scientists think of much more than wrinkles. They think of an organ with multitudes of microbes, immune cells, structural proteins and chemical signals that constantly interact with one another.

mix_items.title: DNA testing shows what's really in Western Australian fish and chip shop 'shark' filets
mix_items.summary: Shark products sold at Western Australian fish-and-chips shops are often labeled too ambiguously or, in some cases, mislabeled, leaving consumers unsure which species they are buying, new Murdoch University research shows.

mix_items.title: A 13-meter rocket hit the Moon: Tasmanian researchers helped track it there
mix_items.summary: A 13-meter (43-foot) Falcon 9 rocket stage struck the moon last month, leaving a crater about 20 meters (66 feet) wide. In the days before impact, University of Tasmania researchers from the School of Natural Sciences were the first in the world to detect the object by radar, helping refine predictions of where it would land.

mix_items.title: Painful periods during adolescence linked to symptoms years earlier
mix_items.summary: More than half of girls participating in the long-term U.S. Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) study developed painful periods (dysmenorrhea) by age 12 or 13, according to new research published in The Lancet Child & Adolescent Health. Black and Hispanic girls were most likely to be affected.

mix_items.title: Alzheimer’s may leave a mark on the brain long before plaques appear
mix_items.summary: Brain changes associated with Alzheimer’s may begin at least seven years before amyloid plaques become detectable with current PET scans. Researchers uncovered the signal by tracking healthy older adults with repeated brain imaging over nearly 20 years. The discovery could help scientists identify Alzheimer’s earlier and suggests that important disease processes may start before visible plaque buildup.

mix_items.title: Physicists test the weak equivalence principle in an orbiting space station
mix_items.summary: The weak equivalence principle (WEP) is central to Einstein's general relativity. It posits that gravity must accelerate everything equally, regardless of what it is made from. For the first time, a team led by Ming-Sheng Zhan at the Wuhan Institute of Physics and Mathematics has tested the principle using clouds of continuously free-falling atoms aboard an orbiting space station.

mix_items.title: A coffee-table-size scorpion roamed Earth before forests existed
mix_items.summary: A meter-long scorpion with massive pincers stalked ancient Britain 415 million years ago, long before forests and the better-known age of giant insects. Its surprising size and possible semi-aquatic lifestyle could reshape ideas about how early arthropods became giants.

mix_items.title: A summer odyssey: Female dotterels seek multiple mates across Northern Europe
mix_items.summary: On a high Norwegian plateau in late May, patches of bare ground begin to appear through the snow, and with them arrive some of Europe's most approachable birds. Eurasian dotterels breed on exposed mountain ridges and Arctic tundra from Scotland, through Scandinavia, to Siberia, and are famously tolerant of people—a trait that has long made them easy prey for hunters. They are unusual in another sense, too.

mix_items.title: Despite years of rain, Blue Mountains forests still haven't recovered from the Black Summer megafires
mix_items.summary: For three years before the Black Summer megafires of 2019–20, cool-season rainfall in southeastern Australia was only half the normal amount. When fires broke out, intensely dry conditions helped them spread through areas typically resistant to burning, such as wetlands and rainforests.

mix_items.title: Seven new species show 250-million-year-old marine group is still evolving
mix_items.summary: Scientists believed there were only two species of hornerid bryozoans in Aotearoa New Zealand, but new research shows several more have been secretly evolving and thriving in the nation's southern waters.

mix_items.title: Psychologists investigate how first impressions influence impressions of trustworthiness
mix_items.summary: First impressions of whether someone appears trustworthy are influenced by the faces we have just seen, according to new research from psychologists at the University of Aberdeen. The study is the first to show that our snap judgments of trustworthiness are not based solely on the face in front of us. Instead, they are subtly shaped by the faces we have encountered only moments earlier.

mix_items.title: New research: Google's AI Overviews reinforce some conspiracy theories
mix_items.summary: Imagine overhearing on a bus that the city council plans to implement new restrictions under an urban planning program called "15-minute cities." Curious, you search the term on Google.

mix_items.title: Understanding the link between hepatitis C and HIV persistence
mix_items.summary: Naglaa Shoukry and Petronela Ancuta, researchers in the Immunopathology Research Theme at the Centre de recherche du CHUM (CRCHUM), are shedding new light on one of the greatest challenges in HIV research: understanding why the virus remains in the body despite treatment.

mix_items.title: More than 120 molecular species found in giant cloud near Milky Way's center
mix_items.summary: Astronomers have discovered a second interstellar cloud near the center of the Milky Way that is extraordinarily rich in complex molecules, including several molecules associated with prebiotic chemistry. The newly studied cloud, G+0.633-0.0604, or G+0.633, contains more than 120 identified molecular species and is the first confirmed chemical twin of another famous molecule-rich cloud. Their paper, posted to the arXiv preprint server on Aug. 14, outlines the chemistry of the newfound cloud.

mix_items.title: First human clinical trial to test precision form of FLASH proton therapy
mix_items.summary: A new form of proton therapy—designed to deliver cancer-killing radiation therapy in less than a second, through fewer sessions, with potentially less risk of damaging side effects—is now being tested in a phase 1 clinical trial at the Abramson Cancer Center of the University of Pennsylvania. Known as FLASH proton therapy, the feasibility study represents the first time that the "conformal," or precise 3D targeting, version of the technique has been tested in human patients in the United States.

mix_items.title: Is sleep training likely to help or harm your baby?
mix_items.summary: Welcoming a baby is a time of great joy for parents. It can also be one of the most challenging. One of the greatest difficulties many parents face is getting their baby to sleep and resettling them following nighttime awakenings.

mix_items.title: Irritability, anxiety and negative thought patterns in ADHD associated with increased depression risk
mix_items.summary: A new study by the Wolfson Center at Cardiff University investigating links between ADHD and depression has shown that underlying factors such as anxiety and negative thought patterns in childhood, adolescence and young adulthood indicate depression risk. The research team suggests that identifying these emotions, behaviors and beliefs in children and young people with ADHD could be a promising intervention for preventing future depression in these individuals.

mix_items.title: Human-like AI not always the answer in customer service
mix_items.summary: The next time something goes wrong with your bank account, package delivery or a bill, there's a good chance you'll be directed to AI for customer service.

mix_items.summary: If you sit in an Australian park or garden for long enough, chances are you might catch a flash of brilliant feathers out of the corner of your eye: the superb fairywren. With its bright blue and soft brown plumage, it was voted Australia’s “bird of the year” in 2021, “narrowly defeating the tawny frogmouth […]

mix_items.title: ‘You can’t protect what you don’t know:’ Interview with marine scientist Loyiso Dunga
mix_items.summary: CAPE TOWN — When scientist Loyiso Dunga began mapping the Great African Seaforest in 2016, he decided to go snorkeling. The South African section of the kelp forest stretches around 800 miles or 1,300 kilometers, straddling two coasts and two oceans. Dunga grew up in a coastal community, Nqabara, in South Africa’s Wild Coast. As […]

mix_items.title: 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck reveals ancient waterproofing secrets
mix_items.summary: Scientists analyzing a 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck found that its hull was coated with pine tar and, in one area, a mixture of tar and beeswax. Pollen trapped in those ancient coatings acted like a geographic fingerprint, revealing the landscapes surrounding the ship when repairs were made.

mix_items.title: A lost mega-cliff may explain the Grand Canyon’s missing billion years
mix_items.summary: A colossal cliff system created as the supercontinent Rodinia broke apart may have exposed the heart of the Grand Canyon nearly a billion years before the Colorado River carved it. The ancient landscape could also help explain why enormous sections of North America’s geological record appear to be missing.

mix_items.title: “One-in-a-million” sea creature fossil preserves soft tissue for 450 million years
mix_items.summary: Scientists have identified exceptionally rare soft tissue preserved in a 450-million-year-old crinoid fossil, more than 200 million years older than the first dinosaurs. Its delicate tube feet offer a remarkable new window into how some of Earth’s earliest reef animals lived, fed, and evolved.

mix_items.title: A new Ice Age species was hiding in la brea tar pits fossils for decades
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered a new extinct amphibian species hiding in the fossil collections of Los Angeles’ La Brea Tar Pits. Named Spea labreae, the Ice Age spadefoot toad is an exceptionally rare find—only one other extinct Pleistocene amphibian has ever been identified in North America. Its bones had been sitting in collections since the 1950s before a researcher noticed features that set it apart from known species.
